messages.subject: censored data
parts:
In a BUGS example (vol 1, Mice), we have right censored lifetime
data (in other words, we only know that the lives of some mice
would be larger than some points). For this example, pretending
we do not have censoring and use stan gm to generate cpp code,
which would be modified to reflect the censoring, I could have the
example running.

When computing the log-likelihood, originally we only have
lp__ += stan::prob::weibull_log(t[i - 1], r,
sigma[group[i - 1] - 1]);

I changed to:

// is_censored are the data indicating not censoring (0)
or right censored (1)
if (0 == is_censored[i - 1])
lp__ += stan::prob::weibull_log(t[i - 1], r,
sigma[group[i - 1] - 1]);
// right censored: log(1 - F(t_r)), where F: weibull CDF
else lp__ += -pow(last_t[i - 1] / sigma[group[i - 1] - 1],
r);

So the example is kind of working if we modify the cpp node.

--
Jiqiang

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] censored [& truncated] data
parts:
We definitely don't want people to have to
modify the C++ code to implement censored or
truncated models. But our models will look
different again from those of BUGS and JAGS.

I don't quite understand their Weibull model,
but here's how it'll work for a normal distro.

First, we can't handle NA values -- all data
must be in the form of an integer or floating point
value. So if y[1:N] is all the data with some
NA values, let

Outcomes and predictor for uncensored values:

data {
double C; // censoring point

int N_uc; // number of uncensored items
double y_uc[1:N_uc]; // measurement of uncensored item
double x_uc[1:N_uc]; // predictors for uncensored items

int N_c; // number of censored items
double x_c[1:N_c]; // predictors for censored items
}
model {
for (n in 1:N_uc)
y_uc[n] ~ normal(alpha * x_uc[n] + beta, sigma);

for (n in 1:N_c)
1 ~ bernoulli(c_normal_lb(alpha * x_c[n] + beta, sigma, C));
}

First, note that although y_uc[n] must be less than
C, this is not a constraint on the variable in the Stan
sense of wanting to transform it. So it remains double
rather than double(,C) in the declaration.

The first sampling is not truncated. This is equivalent
in terms of contribution to log likelihood to:

0 ~ bernoulli(...);
y_uc[n] ~ normal_ub(alpha * x_uc[n] + beta, sigma, C);

Andrew and Jennifer do a bunch of these calcs in their book.

What's needed in Stan to make this fly:

1. All the cumulative distributions. For instance,
c_normal_lb(mu,sigma,L) needs to be included as a special
function and defined to be Pr[X > L] if X ~ normal(mu,sigma).

You'll of course need the Weibull. All the necessary
cumulative distributions are in Boost and we'll use the
densities in Stan for their derivatives. So it's a fair
bit of work per density for all of this.

2. Allowing general expressions on the LHS of samples (as
in the 1 above). Very unusual from a BUGS perspective, but
no obstacle for Stan. I'll fix that right now and post when
I've done it.

If you want, you can also sample latent parameters
y_c, as in:

for (n in 1:N_c) {
y_hat <- alpha * x_c[n] + beta;
1 ~ bernoulli(c_normal_lb(y_hat,sigma,C));
y_c[n] ~ normal_lb(y_hat,sigma,C);
}

Then they can play with others. In this case, it might also
be conceptually clearer (though less computationally efficient)
to have parallel loops:

for (n in 1:N_uc) {
y_uc[n] ~ normal_ub(alpha * x_uc[n] + beta, sigma, C);
0 ~ bernoulli(c_normal_ub(alpha * x_uc[n] + beta, sigma, C));
}

for (n in 1:N_c) {
y_c[n] ~ normal_lb(alpha * x_c[n] + beta, sigma, C);
1 ~ bernoulli(c_normal_lb(alpha * x_c[n] + beta, sigma, C);
}

I'll probably present it this way and then note that the top loop
simplifes to how I wrote it at first, and you can drop the y_c[n]
sampling if you don't need it.

- Bob
